title: Election Commission's SIR exercise identifies just 1,600 foreigners on voter lists in six states
shows: Hindustan Times reports that it approached the Chief Electoral Officers of 26 states and union territories where the revision was complete or a draft roll had been published, and that officials in 11 of them answered. Six gave a count of suspected foreign nationals, about 1,600 in all among some 9.86 crore electors. By the paper's account they were 716 in Karnataka, about 500 in Kerala, 419 suspected foreign passport holders in Goa, three in Jharkhand, two in Meghalaya and none in Mizoram. Officials in Punjab, Delhi, Uttarakhand and Telangana said they kept no such figure, and an official in Odisha said cases were found and not counted. The paper quotes a senior official of the Commission saying that states were not asked to collect the figure separately and that such cases went under the category Others. It sets these counts beside the Commission's press note of 24 June 2025, which named the inclusion of foreign illegal immigrants among the reasons for the revision.
quote: States were not asked to collect this data separately. We also don’t have combined or state-wise data on this. If any such cases came up, they were placed under the ‘Others’ category in ASDDO. But ECI has not asked them to provide these details,
note: Published 29 October 2026 at 12:47 am IST, updated 7:09 am, by Himanshi Dahiya, with the full text served on the page. This is the report The Wire's piece of 29 October 2026, 'BJP and EC Said SIR Was to Remove Infiltrators. A Report Shows it Recorded Just 1,600 Foreigners' (The Wire Staff), relies on, and The Wire adds nothing to it beyond Amit Shah's remark of 2025 and its own words that the SIR 'has now deleted 13 crore names', so the original is listed in its place. The 1,600 is not an official figure and no official document gives it. It is the paper's own sum of counts given to it by officials of six Chief Electoral Officers' offices (716 + about 500 + 419 + 3 + 2 + 0 = about 1,640), and the senior Commission official it quotes says the Commission holds no combined or state-wise figure. The Karnataka 716 is attributed to an official of the state Chief Electoral Officer's office, and the Chief Electoral Officer himself said only that the number was less than 1,000. The News Minute of 29 October credits the 716 to the Times of India. The roll figures the paper gives agree with data/india/states.json: Karnataka 99.7 lakh fewer on the final roll (99,76,625 general electors), Kerala 8,97,211 and Goa 1,27,468 fewer, Meghalaya 1,65,682 fewer and a final roll of 21.8 lakh, Mizoram about 39,000 fewer (39,199), Jharkhand 2.646 crore before and 43.6 lakh left off the draft. The 9.86 crore is the sum of the six states' latest rolls (Karnataka final, Jharkhand draft, the other four final). The Reporters' Collective's piece of 16 October 2026 on the absence of any foreigner category is already on the reading list.

title: Five Reasons Why the ECI’s Explanation for 16 Lakh Appeals Against Bengal Voters Falls Short
shows: Aparna Bhattacharya reads paragraph 63 of the Commission's counter-affidavit of 26 October 2026, which says that officers of the office of West Bengal's Chief Electoral Officer filed the appeals against 16.10 lakh voters cleared by judicial officers, in their capacity as authorities under the Representation of the People Act. She sets out five problems with that account. The appellate tribunals were created by the Supreme Court and do not exist under the Act, and the orders of 1 April and 6 April 2026 that the affidavit quotes name no officer. The affidavit lists the CEO, DEOs, EROs and AEROs as the authorities for the rolls and does not say that any of them filed the appeals. Appeal records collected by the Civic Research Group and analysed by The Wire show more than 12 lakh of the appeals in one batch lodged on 5 April, a day before the order of 6 April. The affidavit describes these voters as already on the rolls with orders in their favour and gives no ground for challenging them. The piece reports that hearing notices of one tribunal in Murshidabad record the appeal as filed by the Additional CEO, and quotes Prasenjit Bose, who chairs the West Bengal Congress SIR committee, calling the appeals prima facie unauthorised and illegal and asking for a judicial probe.
quote: Read against the claims made by the ECI in this affidavit, the court’s orders as well as the appeal records, the above explanation leaves five problems unresolved.
note: Read in full from The Wire's own post data (post date 28 October 2026, 3:02 pm, by Aparna Bhattacharya). Every claim in the summary is the piece's. The piece gives two dates for the tribunals: it says the Supreme Court ordered them on 10 March and the Commission notified 19 of them on 20 March, and it quotes Bose saying they were created in April 2026. The affidavit is court-52 in disputes_research/courts.json. The affidavit itself was not read, so paragraphs 55, 60, 61, 62 and 63 are as the piece quotes them. Her earlier piece of 24 October on the timing of the same appeals, using the same Civic Research Group records, is already on the reading list, and The Indian Express editorial of 28 October (round 28) reads the same paragraph of the affidavit.

title: Six Ways EC Affidavit Ends Up Reinforcing Doubts About SIR Irregularities and Commission's Functioning
shows: Sravasti Dasgupta reads the Commission's affidavit of 26 October 2026 against The Indian Express's reports that Election Commissioners Vivek Joshi and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu objected 14 times in ten months, and finds that it denies none of those findings. By her account the affidavit says the Commission neither released nor authorised the release of any internal note, and that all three orders for the SIR were reached unanimously. It denies that Form 6 was amended while accepting that the declaration was entered into the online page of the form, and it now calls the declaration a separate and independent document, where a press note of the month before had said the declaration attached to Form 6 was upheld by the Supreme Court. She writes that on Goa it says 88 of the 97 voters have applied again through Form 6 and does not explain why registration officers could not restore them, and that on West Bengal it says the appeals were not brought to the Commission. It announces a committee with experts from IIT Mumbai and IISc Bengaluru to review new ECINet modules without mentioning that Joshi had proposed one, and it calls the complaint the two Commissioners sent to the Cabinet Secretary about a work allocation order misconceived, saying the order was never implemented.
quote: A close reading of the affidavit shows that the Election Commission has actually not denied any of the findings in the Indian Express‘s report.
note: Read in full from The Wire's own post data (post date 28 October 2026, 12:56 am, by Sravasti Dasgupta). Every claim in the summary is the piece's. The piece gives 97 Goa voters in one place and 98 in another, and says in one place that the 88 re-applied and in another that they had been added back. The Commission's affidavit as The Indian Express reported it, and The Indian Express editorial of 28 October (round 28), give 88 of 97 who applied through Form 6. The piece says Form 6 can only be amended by Parliament, while the affidavit as Bar and Bench reported it says only the Central Government can amend it. 'IIT Mumbai' is the piece's name for the institute. The affidavit is court-52 in disputes_research/courts.json and was not itself read.

title: India: Mass Voter Roll Exclusions Deeply Flawed
shows: Human Rights Watch says it interviewed 70 people in Delhi, West Bengal, Maharashtra and Karnataka from August 2026, among them 40 whose families were affected by the revision, former election commissioners, lawyers, activists and a serving electoral official. It finds that people were excluded for mismatched names, spelling errors, having six or more siblings or siblings born less than nine months apart, and that the software flagged Adivasi and Muslim names disproportionately because their spellings vary. It reports families who lost passport renewals, food rations, a West Bengal cash transfer for women, scholarships and residence certificates after their names were left off, including people whose appeals were still pending. It describes the bulk use of Form 7 against Muslim voters as the media reported it, transgender people excluded because their documents carry different names, and security forces beating and arresting protesters in October 2026. Its Asia director, Elaine Pearson, calls for the revision to be scrapped and for everyone wrongly excluded to regain the vote promptly.
quote: Indian authorities first stripped millions of citizens of their right to vote and are now beating and jailing them for peacefully protesting these rights violations,
note: Published 28 October 2026 at 11:30 pm EDT (29 October in India), datelined London, and labelled Report on the page. It is a news release presenting the organisation's own interviews, and no separate report document was linked from it. Every finding in the summary is the organisation's, and the interviewees it quotes are not named here. Its figures set against data/india/states.json: the 'over 130 million names' it calls removed are the names left off the drafts, 13,39,03,307 in 31 states. Its 'nearly 4.7 million' for Bihar matches the fall from the roll before to the final roll, 47,73,025. Its 93% of decided West Bengal appeals restored, given without a source, agrees with the Congress graphic The Hindu reported on 27 October and differs from the 91.13% the Internet Freedom Foundation took from an RTI reply. It dates the West Bengal Assembly election April 2025 in one sentence. The election was held in April 2026. The Patharpratima figure of over 92% Muslim among those deleted is given without a source on the page.

title: Before UP polls, let’s ask: Does voter list meet criteria of completeness, equity, accuracy
shows: Jean Drèze and Yogendra Yadav put Uttar Pradesh's adult population at an estimated 16.2 crore on 1 March 2026 against 13.4 crore names on the final roll of April 2026, down from 15.4 crore before the revision, and conclude that about 2.8 crore voters, or 17.3% of adults, appear to be missing. They reply to Surjit Bhalla's estimate of a shortfall of 20 lakh, which treats all non-enrolment as voluntary and builds on the 40% of the state's adults aged 18 to 29 who were not enrolled in 2024, and say that with the figure for 2019 his shortfall would be 93 lakh. As further evidence they cite the State Election Commission's parallel revision of the rural roll, which ended at 12.6 crore and, with the unrevised urban list of 2023, gives 16.9 crore voters in the state. They hold that the final roll fails on completeness, equity and accuracy, and that the shortfall works against women and young voters.
quote: Thus, any significant shortfall from the adult population is an administrative failure to be examined and rectified.
note: On-page headline 'Before UP polls, let’s ask: Does voter list meet criteria of completeness, equity, accuracy'. The browser title of the same page is 'UP voter list: 2.8 crore adults missing from electoral rolls'. Published 29 October 2026 at 6:20 am IST by Jean Drèze and Yogendra Yadav, with the full text served on the page. The piece describes Drèze as visiting professor in the Department of Economics, Ranchi University, and Yadav as a member of Swaraj India and national convenor of the Bharat Jodo Abhiyan. Their figures agree with data/india/states.json for Uttar Pradesh: roll before 15,44,30,092 (their 15.4 crore), final roll 13,39,84,792 on 10 April 2026 (their 13.4 crore), adults projected for 2026 16,16,85,000 (their 16.2 crore). On those figures the adults projection less the final roll is 2,77,00,208, 17.1% of adults. Their 17.3% is 2.8 crore over 16.2 crore. Later in the piece they give the adult population as 16.1 crore. Their 2.8 crore is a different measure from the 2,88,74,067 left off the draft, and the final roll is 2,04,45,300 below the roll before. Their column of 20 October and both Surjit Bhalla pieces they answer (17 and 24 October) are already on the reading list.

title: The SIR verdict, serious constitutional questions
shows: Bishwajit Bhattacharyya, a Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court and a former Additional Solicitor General of India, argues that the Court erred in its verdict of 27 May 2026 by allowing the Commission a limited inquiry into citizenship when it includes or deletes names. In his reading the words limited and strict sense carry no legal significance, and the holding that the Commission's power affects an individual's entitlement to be on the roll can only mean that it may disenfranchise an existing voter. He says the Commission's role in preparing the roll is ministerial, that the verdict named no document as proof of citizenship, and that a qualified voter can be disqualified only on the grounds in Article 326 and only after a hearing. He asks how a roll used in a concluded election can be altered on suspicion, and asks the Court to lay down a yardstick for establishing citizenship and to hold the right to vote a basic feature of the Constitution.
quote: How can an electoral roll used in a concluded election be altered on the grounds of suspicion? How can a person be disenfranchised after having voted in the previous election?
note: Lead article, published 29 October 2026 at 12:16 am IST and updated 12:38 pm, by Bishwajit Bhattacharyya, described at its foot as Senior Advocate, Supreme Court of India and a former Additional Solicitor General of India. The page marks itself as not free to read and asks the reader to register, so it is marked as needing a subscription or sign-in. The full text was read from the article body the page carries in its structured data. Every argument in the summary is the author's. The verdict of 27 May 2026 is the Supreme Court's judgment on the Bihar SIR, linked from the article at api.sci.gov.in. His view that the three judgments he cites raise the right to vote to a basic feature is given as his own interpretation.

title: SIR: Karnataka 64.5 lakh voters ‘short’; foreign nationals still ‘uncounted’
shows: The News Minute applies the Chief Electoral Officer's elector to population ratio of 66.11 to a projected Karnataka population of about 6.89 crore on 1 March 2026, of whom about 5.19 crore would be old enough to vote, and finds the final roll of 4,54,55,689 general electors about 64.5 lakh short. By its calculation 38.41 lakh of them, or 59.5%, are aged 18 to 29. It reports the Chief Electoral Officer, V. Anbu Kumar, saying that out of more than 43.82 lakh notices for logical discrepancies and unmapped entries at least 1,88,324 names were deleted from the final roll, with 61,867 marked ineligible, and that the foreign nationals found number less than a thousand with the count still under way. It cites the Times of India for a figure of 716 foreign nationals, and reports that the Commission has ordered special drives and a fresh look at constituencies, wards and booths where deletions were high.
quote: Identifying foreign nationals was among the stated aims of the country-wide SIR, but in Karnataka, as in other states, the number of foreign nationals was never publicly released by ECI officials.
note: Published 29 October 2026 by TNM Staff, with the full text served on the page. It says The Hindu used the same population projections (the 2020 Report of the Technical Group on Population Projections) for different age groups, which suggests the calculation follows The Hindu's. Its figures agree with data/karnataka/summary.json and data/india/states.json: final roll 4,54,55,689 general electors, adults projected for 2026 5,19,06,000 (its 5.19 crore), so the shortfall of 64.5 lakh is the adults projection less the final roll. Its 21.8% dead and duplicate among the 1.08 crore left off the draft matches 23,49,734 of 1,07,96,339, and its 8.2 lakh net additions match 8,19,714. Its other total, 99,32,303 fewer from 5,54,32,314 to 4,55,00,011, counts the final roll with service electors (4,55,00,011). On general electors the fall is 99,76,625. Hindustan Times of the same day attributes the 716 to an official of the Chief Electoral Officer's office.
